Christoph Wittich
kris'tof vit'ik
n. (Christoph Wittich, 1625–1687, Cartesian theologian at Duisburg, Nijmegen and Leiden)
Greek Christophoros, Christ-bearer; German Wittich, from a Germanic personal name.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Christoph Wittich was the most able of the Cartesian theologians in the Dutch universities, and the dictionary names his central proposal and rejects it. Where the Scriptures describe the sun rising, the earth standing fast, or the heavens as a tent, Wittich held that the Holy Ghost was accommodating himself to the common speech and mistaken notions of the vulgar, so that such statements carry no truth about the natural world at all. The motive was to shield Scripture from the new astronomy. The cost was a principle with no boundary: once a class of statements is exempted from truth-telling because the audience would not have understood better, there is nothing to stop the exemption spreading. Our Lord treats the smallest mark of the text as unbreakable (Mat 5:18).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines accommodation as adjustment or adaptation, and tittle as a small particle, a minute part, a jot.

expand to see more

ACCOMMODA'TION, n. Fitness; adaptation; adjustment of differences; reconciliation.

TIT'TLE, n. A small particle; a minute part; a jot; an iota.

VUL'GAR, a. Pertaining to the common unlettered people; plebeian; common.

INFALLIBIL'ITY, n. The quality of being incapable of error or mistake; entire exemption from liability to error.

Key Scripture

Mat 5:18 — "For verily I say unto you, Till heaven and earth pass, one jot or one tittle shall in no wise pass from the law, till all be fulfilled."

Joh 10:35 — "If he called them gods, unto whom the word of God came, and the scripture cannot be broken;"

Psa 12:6 — "The words of the LORD are pure words: as silver tried in a furnace of earth, purified seven times."

Modern Corruption

He exempted Scripture's language about nature from truth-telling, to protect it.

expand to see more

The error is named by its proper name: accommodation, in the strong sense that makes some of Scripture's statements untrue but harmless. Wittich proposed it to defend the Bible from the astronomers; the result is a Bible that speaks truly only where its readers already agree. Nineteenth-century liberalism applied exactly this principle to the miracles, to the creation account, and at length to the resurrection, and it was able to do so because the exemption Wittich introduced carried no limit within itself. The dictionary distinguishes this from the ordinary and legitimate observation that Scripture speaks in human language and from the standpoint of the observer, which it certainly does.

The principle to recover is that the whole text is true, down to its smallest mark, and that nothing in it is exempt. “Till heaven and earth pass, one jot or one tittle shall in no wise pass from the law, till all be fulfilled” (Mat 5:18). Our Lord argues from an incidental word of a psalm and adds that “the scripture cannot be broken” (Joh 10:35). The purity is total: “The words of the LORD are pure words: as silver tried in a furnace of earth, purified seven times” (Psa 12:6).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek iota (G2503), the smallest Hebrew letter; Greek keraia (G2762), a little horn, the stroke that distinguishes a letter.

expand to see more

Greek iota (G2503) — the letter iota, the smallest letter; Matthew 5:18.

Greek keraia (G2762) — a little horn, a tiny stroke of a letter; Matthew 5:18.

Greek luo (G3089) — to loose, to break, to dissolve; John 10:35.

Hebrew tsaraph (H6884) — to refine, to try as metal; Psalm 12:6.

Greek theopneustos (G2315) — God-breathed, inspired of God; 2 Timothy 3:16.

Usage

"“one jot or one tittle shall in no wise pass from the law” (Mat 5:18) — no exempted class of statements."

"“the scripture cannot be broken” (Joh 10:35) — argued from one incidental word."

"“The words of the LORD are pure words” (Psa 12:6) — purified seven times, not partly."
